name: TRT clinics (online telehealth)

lead: TRT clinics, increasingly online, evaluate men for low testosterone and prescribe testosterone replacement therapy. Looksmaxxers turn to them as a route to TRT, hoping for more muscle, less fat and a more masculine look.

TRT supplements or replaces the body's own androgen and is a standard treatment for hypogonadism. Reference sources note it is also prescribed for age-related decline, which they call controversial. They give little information specific to telehealth clinics, and appearance outcomes are less studied than treatment of diagnosed low testosterone.

paras: Patients typically get bloodwork, a consultation and a prescription, then follow-up labs on a regular schedule. Testosterone comes as injection, gel, patch, pellet or other forms, and users generally treat it as long-term therapy.

Wikipedia lists possible risks of TRT including higher hematocrit, worsened sleep apnea, accelerated growth of existing prostate cancer, possible clot risk and suppressed spermatogenesis, and says PSA and hematocrit should be monitored. TRT is a controlled prescription therapy, and clinic quality varies.

chain: More muscle, leaner, more masculine look
angle.text: TRT clinics prescribe testosterone so circulating levels rise, which users expect to support muscle, leanness and a more masculine look. Clinical evidence covers treating diagnosed low testosterone; appearance outcomes and telehealth providers are less studied.

lead: TRT clinics are medical practices, many of them operating online, that assess men for low testosterone and prescribe testosterone replacement therapy (TRT). In appearance communities, TRT is discussed as a route to more muscle, less body fat, fuller body and facial hair and a more masculine look, and clinics are the access point for men who want a prescription.[1][2][3]

TRT supplements or replaces the body's androgens and can be delivered by injection, gel, patch, pellet or other forms.[1] Wikipedia describes it as the classic treatment for male hypogonadism, a condition in which impaired muscle and body-hair development are among the recognised signs.[1][4] Prescribing for age-related changes is described as controversial and under study.[1]

The clinic model typically involves a symptom questionnaire, morning blood tests and a prescription, with follow-up monitoring of values such as PSA and hematocrit.[1][4] Telehealth, the use of electronic communication for remote clinical care, grew sharply during COVID-19, and online platforms for other men's health conditions such as erectile dysfunction have been the subject of published commentary.[5][6] Lifter forums such as T Nation have discussed online providers, local clinics and the quality of monitoring they offer.[3][7][8]
infobox: Injection, gel, patch, pellet and others[1]
AUA supports a low-testosterone diagnosis below 300 ng/dL total[4]

paras: A TRT clinic is a prescriber-led service. Diagnosis rests on symptoms plus a morning blood test, since testosterone levels fall by as much as 13 percent across the day and reference ranges are based on morning values.[4] The American Urological Association supports a diagnosis when total testosterone is below 300 ng/dL, and treatment is often considered below 230 ng/dL with symptoms. LH is checked as well, because testosterone is usually not used when LH is low (secondary or tertiary hypogonadism).[4]

Online clinics deliver these steps through video or phone consultations and mail-in or lab-partner blood draws. Telehealth more broadly is defined as remote clinical care and education using telecommunications, and its use expanded greatly during COVID-19, when US primary care telemedicine visits rose from about 1.4 million in Q2 2019 to about 35 million in Q2 2020.[5]

Wikipedia lists oral, buccal, transdermal, injectable and implant testosterone products, and notes alternatives such as hCG (which stimulates testosterone production and is used by men who want to keep fertility) and low-dose clomifene.[4] Which options a clinic offers is a point of discussion among patients on forums.[3][7]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting communities
paras: On T Nation, posters have described the telehealth market as growing quickly, with one healthcare worker saying telemedicine is not inherently a problem but questioning how some online 'T mills' operate.[3] Another thread has a poster considering moving from an endocrinologist to a TRT clinic because of how many blood markers were being tested.[7] A user who later said they were opening a TRT clinic described the personal impact of TRT as the reason.[8]
Another poster described taking a clinic's phone call after learning of TRT through a weightlifting forum.[9]

The FDA investigated stroke and heart attack reports in 2014 and in 2015 said safety and benefit had not been established for low testosterone due to aging, requiring label warnings. In 2025, after the TRAVERSE trial, it removed the boxed warning while continuing to monitor risks such as blood pressure increases.[1] Nevada banned TRT for UFC fighters in 2014.[1] In the US, the Ryan Haight Act (2008) requires a face-to-face or valid telemedicine consultation before controlled-substance prescriptions, and state licensure rules affect where telehealth practitioners can treat patients.[5]

Wikipedia lists possible TRT risks including raised hematocrit, worsened sleep apnea, effects on existing prostate cancer, possible clot risk and suppressed spermatogenesis, and says PSA and hematocrit should be monitored.[1] The hypogonadism article adds gynecomastia as a possible side effect and describes short- and medium-term TRT as not appearing to raise cardiovascular events, with long-term safety not yet established.[4]

No studies found on online TRT clinics as a category. A 2021 Journal of Urology editorial examined online telehealth platforms for erectile dysfunction, a related direct-to-consumer men's health model.[6] For TRT itself, Wikipedia reports that a 2024 Cochrane review found little clinically meaningful short-term erectile benefit over placebo, that hypogonadal men may see modest improvements in sexual function, mood and energy, and that the TRAVERSE trial found no increased cardiovascular risk versus placebo in men with hypogonadism.[1]

lore.intro: TRT clinics come up on lifter forums as both a convenient route to treatment and a topic of debate about testing thoroughness and prescribing practices.[3][7][8]
